figures.alt: The developer's site plan for 128 Boulder Lane, with labels added by the digest. A pink line encloses everything the plan builds, in a band on the east side of the site: 40 townhomes at the north end, nearest Kennel Hill Drive, then the assisted living and memory care building and its parking toward Route 128, and a driveway out to Boulder Lane at the southeast corner. figures.alt: Map of Centerville. The 128 Boulder Lane parcel sits on the north side of Route 128 at the Wenham line. Boulder Lane runs along the highway from Grapevine Road at the Route 128 interchange. Hull Street and Centerville Elementary School are to the west, and Beverly Commons conservation land is south of the highway.
figures.caption: The Beverly parcel, shaded. Boulder Lane, outlined, runs along Route 128 from Grapevine Road.

land_notes.text: The parcel is wooded and is not conservation land. Its closest neighbors are house lots on Fieldstone Lane and Kennel Hill Drive. Conservation land held by the city and by the Essex County Greenbelt Association lies a few hundred feet away along Boulder Lane.

zoning_notes.text: The parcel is in the IR district, meant mainly for offices, research labs and light industry, which are allowed there without special approval. Two uses for older residents need a special permit from the Zoning Board: what the zoning calls subsidized elderly housing, and a state-licensed nursing home. Assisted living is not listed.

Subsidized elderly housing means at least 80% of the units have a resident 55 or older, at least 15% are permanently affordable, and at least 10% are built for people with disabilities. It doesn't mean the whole building is subsidized.

The whole parcel is in the Water Supply Protection Overlay District. Multifamily housing there needs a Planning Board special permit, which the board may grant only if the project does not harm water quality.
The three neighboring Beverly parcels in the project property are zoned R15, for single-family houses.
Beverly's wetland rules keep most buildings at least 50 feet from a wetland and 100 feet from a vernal pool, a small pond that dries out in summer, where salamanders and wood frogs breed.

history.title: The city takes the property
history.what: Mayor Cahill asked the City Council to take the property by eminent domain (Order #119) and to approve $8 million for it (Order #120): $2 million from free cash and $6 million borrowed. The letter listed three purposes: keep the 108 public parking spaces behind the building that the city had long leased, house city offices during a City Hall renovation of about 24 months, and possibly build affordable housing. It said the city would likely sell the building later

history.title: The Council approves the purchase
history.what: After a public hearing, the Council approved both orders 8-0, with one councilor absent. The agreed payment was $7,350,000, against a December 2022 appraisal of $7,100,000, in exchange for the owners waiving all claims

history.title: Paying down the purchase
history.what: The Council approved moving $2.5 million of free cash toward the purchase (Order #093), 7-0. The finance director said about $2 million would stay as a short-term note until the building was sold
